meta.provenance: First-party editorial draft authored from general horticultural knowledge (university extension literature, Johnny's resistance code conventions). Every row needs human verification before publication; treat as seed data, not citable fact.
meta.scope: Common North American home-garden vegetable pests, diseases, and cultivar-level resistance examples

verification.diseases: All 27 rows verified against extension/APS sources with per-row citations, diagnostic tells, survival data, and seed-borne flags (2026-08-12)
verification.cultivars: Original rows checked against live Johnny's product pages 2026-08-12; 5 not in current catalog flagged unverified; verified and new rows carry scraped HR/IR codes with race sets, days to maturity, Latin name, and product URL
verification.pests: All 25 rows verified against extension sources with per-row citations, identification, scouting thresholds, and phenology/degree-day benchmarks (2026-08-12); 7 corrections applied
verification.gap_fill: 8 diseases and 6 pests added from extension sources with citations; regional severity notes attached where relevance is geographic (2026-08-12)
verification.growing: Growing sub-objects (germination, depth, spacing, sowing method, maturity basis) scraped from Johnny's Growing Information blocks for all johnnyseeds-sourced cultivar rows; 9 fruit cultivars added (2026-08-12). Growing data is crop-level on Johnny's side; per-cultivar fields are maturity, Latin name, and resistance codes.

biology.lifecycle: Overwinters as eggs on Prunus species in cold climates; asexual live-bearing generations all season on vegetables. Winged forms disperse when colonies crowd.
biology.feeding: Phloem sap, undersides of leaves and growing tips

pests.damage: Leaf curling, stunting, honeydew and sooty mold; economic damage is usually from virus transmission rather than direct feeding.
pests.favoring_conditions: Mild weather (18-25 C), lush nitrogen-fed growth, absence of natural enemies after broad-spectrum sprays.
management: Insecticidal soap or horticultural oil on colonies
Conserve lady beetles, lacewings, syrphids, parasitoid wasps
pests.identification: Slender light green to yellowish aphid about 2 mm; winged adults show a dusky dorsal abdominal blotch, and the antennal tubercles converge toward each other, the key separator from other garden aphids.
pests.scouting: No formal treatment threshold. Colonies start on the lowest leaves and move upward, so check lower leaf undersides first and act early, because the economic risk is virus spread rather than visible feeding damage.
pests.phenology: Overwinters as eggs on Prunus in cold climates. Populations build during mild spring weather before temperatures reach 80-85 F, decline in midsummer heat, and rebound in fall.

biology.lifecycle: Continuous asexual reproduction in warm climates; tolerates heat better than most aphids.
biology.feeding: Undersides of leaves, growing points

pests.damage: Curled, yellowed leaves, honeydew on fruit; transmits mosaic viruses in cucurbits.
pests.favoring_conditions: Hot weather; outbreaks common after pyrethroid use kills natural enemies.
pests.identification: Small aphid about 1.5 mm, ranging from yellowish green to bluish gray or nearly black; winged and wingless forms occur together in dense colonies on leaf undersides.
pests.scouting: No established economic threshold. UC IPM suggests yellow sticky cards before planting, then direct foliage checks once aphids appear on traps.
pests.phenology: Unlike most aphids, populations do not collapse in hot weather and can persist into September and October in warm regions.

biology.lifecycle: Gray-green waxy colonies on brassicas only; overwinters as eggs on crop debris in cold areas.
biology.feeding: Dense colonies on leaf undersides and in heads

pests.damage: Contaminates heads and florets, curls leaves, stunts young plants.
pests.favoring_conditions: Cool weather, fall brassica plantings, overwintered crop residue nearby.
management: Insecticidal soap penetrating the wax with repeat applications
pests.identification: Gray-green aphid dusted with waxy bloom that makes colonies look powdery white, dark head, short cornicles; found only on brassicas.
pests.scouting: Treat when more than 10 percent of plants carry at least one aphid, or sample 10 leaves at 10 sites and treat above 20 percent infested leaves. Drop the threshold once the harvested portion begins forming.
pests.phenology: First winged aphids typically appear by early to mid June; the damaging populations land on fall brassica plantings near overwintered residue.

biology.lifecycle: Adults overwinter under debris; bronze egg clusters on leaf undersides from early summer; gray nymphs feed in groups.
biology.feeding: Piercing-sucking on leaves, vines, and fruit

pests.damage: Wilting and blackening of leaves (toxic saliva), collapse of young plants; can vector cucurbit yellow vine disease (Serratia marcescens).
pests.favoring_conditions: Mulch and debris that shelter adults, warm dry seasons, Cucurbita maxima and pumpkins preferred over other cucurbits.
pests.identification: Eggs are shiny bronze-copper ellipses about 1.5 mm laid in evenly spaced clusters of roughly 20 to 40 on leaf undersides; nymphs are gray with black legs and feed in tight groups.
pests.scouting: Action threshold is one egg mass or one adult per plant. Check leaf undersides weekly from the time vines start running through flowering.
pests.phenology: Overwintered adults become active and begin laying as vines run in early summer. Egg to adult takes about 6 to 8 weeks, giving one generation in the north and two to three further south.

biology.lifecycle: Day-flying wasp-mimic moth lays eggs singly at stem bases in early summer; larva bores into the stem for 4-6 weeks, then pupates in soil.
biology.feeding: Larvae tunnel inside vines

pests.damage: Sudden wilt of a whole vine; frass like wet sawdust at entry holes near the base.
pests.favoring_conditions: Prior-year cucurbits in the same soil; thick-stemmed C. maxima and zucchini are most attacked, butternut (C. moschata) largely resistant.
management: Succession plant in early July after flight
Till in fall to destroy pupae
pests.identification: Adult is a day-flying wasp mimic with red-orange and olive-black coloring; larvae are cream-white grubs inside stems, marked externally by wet-sawdust frass at entry holes near the base.
pests.scouting: Begin checking stem bases for frass and entry holes around 1000 degree-days base 50 F, then weekly through the flight period.
pests.phenology: Overwinters as a pupa in soil. Adults fly late June into mid July in the north near 1000 DD50, with a possible partial second flight in late August, or two full generations in the south.

biology.lifecycle: Adults overwinter in field edges and move to seedlings at emergence; larvae feed on cucurbit roots.
biology.feeding: Adults on cotyledons, leaves, flowers, fruit rind; larvae on roots

pests.damage: Defoliation of seedlings, scarred fruit; primary vector of bacterial wilt of cucurbits, which is usually the lethal outcome.
pests.favoring_conditions: Early warm springs, fields with cucurbit history, heavily attracted to cucurbitacin-rich varieties.
management: Delayed planting past overwintered adult flight
Trap crops of Blue Hubbard squash on borders
pests.identification: Adult about 5 mm, yellow-orange with three black longitudinal stripes on the elytra and a black head; larvae are slender white grubs on roots and stems below the soil line.
pests.scouting: Scout twice weekly from emergence through the five-leaf stage. Treat near one beetle per plant on cucumber and melon, lower on wilt-susceptible cucumbers, since wilt risk climbs sharply with beetle density.
pests.phenology: Overwintered adults become active and seek hosts once daytime temperatures reach about 54 to 62 F. That first flight, not a degree-day sum, is the scouting trigger, because even light early feeding can seed bacterial wilt.

biology.lifecycle: Adults overwinter in soil; orange egg masses on leaf undersides; humpbacked red-orange larvae do most feeding.
biology.feeding: Chewing, complete defoliation possible

pests.damage: Defoliation; 20 percent-plus yield loss when defoliation occurs during tuber bulking. Notorious for insecticide resistance.
pests.favoring_conditions: Continuous potato or eggplant culture, warm springs; eggplant is the most attractive garden host.
management: Rotate 200+ meters from last year's solanaceous ground
Spinosad or Bt tenebrionis on small larvae, rotated to avoid resistance
pests.identification: Adult about 10 mm, oval, cream to yellow-orange with ten black longitudinal stripes; larvae are humpbacked and orange-red with two rows of black spots per side, four instars over 2 to 3 weeks.
pests.scouting: Walk a V pattern checking 30 to 50 plants per stop. Common thresholds are 0.5 to 1.0 adults per plant, 4 small larvae per plant, or 1.0 to 1.5 large larvae per plant, since fourth instars do most of the defoliation.
pests.phenology: In New York, overwintered adults emerge April to May, first generation May to July, partial second generation August to September. Pepper is a documented but distinctly secondary host relative to potato, tomato, and eggplant.

biology.lifecycle: Large sphinx moths lay single green eggs; caterpillar reaches 8-10 cm over 3-4 weeks, then pupates in soil.
biology.feeding: Chewing foliage from the top of the plant down, also gouges green fruit

pests.damage: Rapid, dramatic defoliation concentrated on upper stems; dark frass pellets below feeding sites.
pests.favoring_conditions: Mid-to-late summer; unnoticed early instars due to camouflage.
management: Leave parasitized hornworms carrying white Cotesia cocoons
pests.identification: Mature larvae reach about 10 cm. Tomato hornworm (M. quinquemaculata) has a black or dark blue horn and white V-shaped side marks; tobacco hornworm (M. sexta) has a red horn and straighter white diagonal stripes. Adult moths differ by abdominal spot pairs: five for tomato hornworm, six for tobacco hornworm. The row's species-to-common-name pairing is correct.
pests.scouting: Larvae are well camouflaged, so scout first for dark frass pellets on leaves and soil below feeding sites. A UV flashlight at night makes the caterpillars fluoresce.
pests.phenology: Typically one generation in the north: adults emerge late spring to early summer, larvae feed 3 to 4 weeks, then overwinter as soil pupae. Warmer regions add a partial second generation.

biology.lifecycle: The everyday white butterfly; yellow bullet eggs laid singly; velvety green larvae feed 2-3 weeks.
biology.feeding: Chewing ragged holes, boring into heads

pests.damage: Holes in leaves, frass contamination in heads and florets.
pests.favoring_conditions: Any season brassicas are present; continuous plantings.
management: Fine mesh netting or row cover for the whole crop cycle
pests.identification: Adult is a white butterfly with a 1.3 to 1.6 inch wingspan and one or two black forewing spots; larvae are velvety green, up to about 1 inch, finely hairy, and keep a full set of prolegs unlike loopers.
pests.scouting: Scout weekly to twice weekly. A commonly used action threshold is about 0.3 larvae per plant, tightened as heads form.
pests.phenology: A degree-day model with a 9.4 C lower threshold predicts larvae roughly 195 GDD after the first adult flight biofix. Two to three generations in Canada, three to five in warmer temperate regions.

biology.lifecycle: Migratory moth, does not overwinter in cold climates; larva loops as it walks (no middle prolegs).
biology.feeding: Chewing large irregular holes

pests.damage: Similar to cabbageworm but wider host range and heavier late-summer feeding.
pests.favoring_conditions: Late summer after migratory buildup.
management: Bt kurstaki (less effective on large larvae)
pests.identification: Larvae are light green with two thin white lateral stripes, tapering toward the head, with only three rear proleg pairs, producing the looping gait; mature larvae exceed 1.5 inches.
pests.scouting: Treat when about 10 percent of plants carry one or more early-instar larvae under a quarter inch. Pheromone traps help time sprays to peak flight.
pests.phenology: The row's non-overwintering claim is confirmed: it overwinters as pupae only in warm southern regions and Mexico. Migrant moths recolonize the north early July through late August, giving roughly 1 to 3 Midwest generations depending on arrival.

biology.lifecycle: Tiny moth, very fast cycle (about 2-4 weeks egg to adult); small green larvae wriggle violently and drop on silk when disturbed.
biology.feeding: Window-pane feeding on leaf undersides

pests.damage: Shot-hole and windowpane leaf damage; worldwide the most insecticide-resistant vegetable pest.
pests.favoring_conditions: Warm dry weather; heavy rain suppresses larvae.
management: Bt rotated with spinosad to manage resistance
pests.identification: Pale green larvae about a third of an inch that wriggle violently and drop on silk when disturbed; feeding leaves a windowpane pattern where only the upper cuticle remains.
pests.scouting: Examine at least 50 plants. Thresholds tighten with crop stage: about 10 percent infested plants at seedling, 30 percent vegetative, but only 5 percent once heads begin forming.
pests.phenology: Does not reliably overwinter where crucifer hosts are absent in winter. Populations rebuild each season from weedy brassicas, crop residue, and long-distance dispersal, which is why residue destruction is emphasized.

biology.lifecycle: Migratory in the north; moths lay eggs on fresh corn silk or on tomato foliage near fruit; larvae enter ear tips or fruit.
biology.feeding: Chewing inside ear tips and fruit

pests.damage: Ear-tip kernels eaten with frass; round holes into tomato fruit near the calyx.
pests.favoring_conditions: Fresh silking corn during moth flights; late plantings hit hardest.
management: Vegetable or Bt oil applied to silks 3-6 days after silk emergence
Early planting to avoid peak flight
pests.identification: Larvae vary from light green or yellow to brown or nearly black, with alternating light and dark longitudinal stripes and microspines giving a rough texture. Cannibalistic, so usually one larva per ear or fruit.
pests.scouting: Set pheromone traps at silk height along field edges from early June or just before silking. Check twice weekly until first catch, then daily. Nightly catches of 20 or more moths signal a spray-worthy flight.
pests.phenology: Development thresholds roughly 55 F lower and 92 to 95 F upper, about 968 degree-days per generation. Does not overwinter north of roughly 40 degrees N, so northern infestations depend on Gulf-state migrants peaking mid July through September.

biology.lifecycle: Overwinters as larva in corn stalks; egg masses on leaf undersides; larvae bore into stalks, ears, and pepper fruit.
biology.generations_per_year: 1-4 by latitude and pheromone race (E/Z strains)
biology.feeding: Boring in stalks, ear shanks, pepper fruit under the cap

pests.damage: Broken tassels and stalks, shot-hole leaf feeding, internal pepper fruit rot from entry wounds.
pests.favoring_conditions: Overwintered corn stubble nearby; regional populations have declined where Bt field corn is widespread.
management: Shred or till corn stalks in fall
Bt kurstaki timed at egg hatch into whorls
pests.identification: Mature larvae are flesh-colored with a dark brown head, three quarters to one inch. Egg masses are white overlapping fish-scale clusters that turn amber-tan with visible black head capsules just before hatch.
pests.scouting: Bait pheromone traps for the local races, an E-strain and a Z-strain lure at least 50 feet apart in weedy borders, since flight timing and generation count differ by race. Pair with weekly whorl scouting for shot-hole feeding.
pests.phenology: Overwinters as a mature larva inside corn stalks and pupates in spring. Univoltine populations fly around July; bivoltine populations fly late May to early June and again in August.

pests.scientific_name: Phyllotreta cruciferae (crucifer flea beetle), Epitrix cucumeris (potato flea beetle), Epitrix fuscula (eggplant flea beetle), Disonycha xanthomelas (spinach flea beetle)

biology.lifecycle: Adults overwinter in litter and attack seedlings in spring; larvae feed on roots; adults jump when disturbed.
biology.feeding: Adults chew tiny round shot-holes in leaves

pests.damage: Shot-hole pitting that can kill seedlings; cosmetic damage on leafy greens; eggplant seedlings especially vulnerable.
pests.favoring_conditions: Hot dry spring weather, weedy brassica field edges, direct-seeded crops emerging into peak adult activity.
management: Transplant larger seedlings instead of direct seeding
Trap crops of radish or mustard
pests.identification: Tiny jumping beetles, 1/16 to 1/2 inch, with enlarged hind femora. Crucifer flea beetle is uniformly shiny black; potato and eggplant flea beetles are brownish black, the eggplant species hairier and duller; the spinach/beet species (Disonycha xanthomelas) is notably larger with a yellow thorax and greenish-black elytra.
pests.scouting: On cole crops, treat once 10 to 20 percent of the stand shows feeding damage. Direct-seeded and seedling stands need earlier action because young plants can die before that threshold.
pests.phenology: Adults overwinter in leaf litter, hedgerows, and wooded edges and move in as soil warms, so damage peaks on emerging or newly transplanted seedlings in warm dry spring weather. One to two generations in the north.

biology.lifecycle: Moths lay eggs on low vegetation and residue; larvae hide in soil by day, feed at night, curl into a C when disturbed.
biology.feeding: Chewing through stems at soil line

pests.damage: Transplants severed at the soil line overnight, mostly within 2 weeks of setting out.
pests.favoring_conditions: Beds recently converted from sod or weedy cover; heavy spring residue.
management: Cardboard or foil stem collars 5 cm into soil
Till 2-3 weeks before planting to starve larvae
pests.identification: Black cutworm larvae are uniformly gray-brown to nearly black with a greasy sheen, up to 2 inches over six instars. Variegated cutworm is grayish with pale spots down the back and a dark W mark on the eighth abdominal segment.
pests.scouting: Weekly, check 25 consecutive plants at each of 10 widely spaced spots for cut stems, then dig near damaged plants to find larvae. Pheromone catches of 2 or more black cutworm moths per trap per night flag a significant egg-laying flight.
pests.phenology: Black cutworm does not reliably overwinter through much of its damaging range; spring moths migrate north. Egg to adult takes 45 or more days, so the transplant-damaging first generation appears a few weeks after the spring flight.

pests.scientific_name: Limonius, Agriotes, Melanotus spp. (click beetle larvae)

biology.lifecycle: Larvae live 2-6 years in soil; worst in ground recently out of sod or pasture.
biology.feeding: Boring into seeds, roots, tubers

pests.damage: Holes and tunnels in potatoes and carrots, poor stands from hollowed seeds.
pests.favoring_conditions: New gardens broken from lawn or grass; cool moist spring soils.
management: Avoid root crops for 2-3 years after breaking sod
Bait traps (buried potato pieces) to assess pressure
pests.identification: Larvae are hard, shiny, wire-like, tan to dark brown, quarter inch to an inch and a quarter, with three pairs of short legs behind the head. Adults are click beetles that snap and flip when placed on their backs.
pests.scouting: Bury bait traps of soaked wheat, corn, or rolled oats 4 to 6 inches deep 2 to 4 weeks before planting once soil at 4 inches exceeds about 50 F, and leave 1 to 2 weeks. An average of one or more wireworms per station is a common action threshold.
pests.phenology: Multi-year larval stage, roughly 2 to 6 years by species, one generation across that span. Damage peaks in spring as soil warms, worst in ground recently out of sod or pasture.

biology.lifecycle: Egg to adult in about 5-14 days by temperature; explosive growth in heat; webs at high density.
biology.feeding: Cell-content feeding on leaf undersides

pests.damage: Stippled bronzed leaves, fine webbing, defoliation in hot spells.
pests.favoring_conditions: Hot dry dusty conditions, drought-stressed plants, broad-spectrum insecticides that kill predatory mites.
management: Overhead water or forceful spray to disrupt colonies
Horticultural oil or insecticidal soap on undersides
pests.identification: Adults about 0.5 mm, oval, pale yellow-green to brown with two dark lateral spots. Overwintering females turn bright orange-red.
pests.scouting: Tap older mid-canopy leaves over white paper and watch for moving specks. By the time stippling or webbing is visible the population is already established.
pests.phenology: Many overlapping generations, egg to adult in as little as 5 days in heat. Overwinters outdoors as diapausing orange-red females under bark, debris, and ground cover, and breeds continuously in greenhouses.

biology.lifecycle: About 2-4 weeks egg to adult; year-round in warm climates and greenhouses, does not overwinter outdoors in cold zones.
biology.feeding: Phloem sap from leaf undersides

pests.damage: Honeydew, sooty mold, irregular fruit ripening, squash silverleaf disorder; devastating as the vector of tomato yellow leaf curl virus.
pests.favoring_conditions: Hot climates, greenhouse transplant production, continuous host availability.
pests.identification: Adults about 1 mm, pale yellow with white wings held roof-like at rest; nymphs are flat translucent-yellow scales on leaf undersides. Bemisia tabaci MEAM1 is the current name for what was described as Bemisia argentifolii, so the row's naming is current.
pests.scouting: Yellow sticky cards at about one per 1,000 square feet plus direct leaf counts. On pepper a threshold near 4 adults per leaf on a random 30-leaf sample has been used; thresholds are not established for most other crops.
pests.phenology: Egg to adult in about 2 to 4 weeks by temperature, continuous overlapping generations where warm, and no outdoor overwintering in cold regions.

biology.lifecycle: Tiny slender insects breeding in flowers and leaf sheaths; egg to adult in about 2-3 weeks; pupate in soil.
biology.feeding: Rasping-sucking on leaves, flowers, fruit

pests.damage: Silvery streaks on onion leaves, scarred fruit; western flower thrips transmits tomato spotted wilt virus.
pests.favoring_conditions: Hot dry weather; onion thrips surge when nearby grain or hay is cut.
management: Remove flowering weeds near susceptible crops
pests.identification: Both are slender straw to yellow-brown insects under 2 mm. Onion thrips has 7-segmented antennae and lacks hairs on the front of the thorax; western flower thrips has 8-segmented antennae and thoracic hairs.
pests.scouting: For onion thrips, count total thrips on 20 to 30 plants and divide by leaf number for a thrips-per-leaf figure. Common action thresholds are about 1 per leaf in onion and 1 to 3 in garlic, though UC notes the per-leaf method is not yet validated in California. Blue or yellow sticky traps track flights.
pests.phenology: Five to eight or more overlapping generations. Note that onion thrips is the only known vector of Iris yellow spot virus, a relationship the current vector_of omits.

pests.scientific_name: Liriomyza sativae, L. trifolii; Pegomya betae (beet leafminer), Pegomya hyoscyami (spinach leafminer)

biology.lifecycle: Flies insert eggs into leaf tissue; larvae mine between leaf surfaces for 1-2 weeks, then drop to soil to pupate.
biology.feeding: Larval mines within the leaf blade

pests.damage: Winding white trails or blotch mines; ruins marketability of leafy greens, mostly cosmetic elsewhere.
pests.favoring_conditions: Spring flights onto chenopod greens; lambsquarters weed reservoirs.
management: Sprays are poorly effective once larvae are inside leaves
pests.identification: Adults are small gray to brown flies about a third of an inch. Pegomya larvae make blotch mines, Liriomyza larvae make winding serpentine mines. Eggs are laid in groups of 4 to 8 on leaf undersides.
pests.scouting: Inspect leaf undersides for egg clusters and early translucent mines before they brown. Row covers only work if they go on before the spring egg-laying flight.
pests.phenology: Pegomya beet and spinach leafminers run a 30 to 40 day cycle, 3 to 4 generations, overwintering as soil pupae with April to May emergence. Liriomyza species run 3 to 6 generations.

biology.lifecycle: A herbivorous lady beetle; copper adults overwinter in debris; yellow spiny larvae skeletonize leaves from below.
biology.feeding: Skeletonizing leaf undersides, lace-like damage

pests.damage: Lacy skeletonized foliage, pod scarring; heaviest mid-to-late summer in eastern North America.
pests.favoring_conditions: Successive bean plantings, mild moist summers.
management: Hand-pick adults, larvae, yellow egg masses
pests.identification: Adults are copper-orange ovals 6 to 8 mm with 16 black spots, easily mistaken for a lady beetle. Larvae are yellow and covered in branching spines; eggs are yellow-orange clusters on leaf undersides.
pests.scouting: Check leaf undersides for yellow egg clusters and spiny larvae from emergence onward. The signature is lacy skeletonizing from below rather than ragged chewed holes.
pests.phenology: Adults overwinter in woodland leaf litter and hedgerows and move into beans in June. Cornell reports two Northeast generations, damage peaking in July and again in late August. Pea is confirmed as an occasional host alongside the preferred bean and soybean.
pests.us_regions: The eastern US is its stronghold: the mid-Atlantic and southern Appalachians see the heaviest pressure, with the range running from Kansas and Nebraska east to the Atlantic and from Ontario and Michigan south to Florida. Moderate summer temperatures with regular rainfall favor it, so it is much less of a problem in the arid West and the Great Plains, and it is largely absent as a garden pest on the Pacific coast.

pests.common_name: Cabbage root maggot / onion maggot / seedcorn maggot
pests.scientific_name: Delia radicum / Delia antiqua / Delia platura

biology.lifecycle: Flies lay eggs at stem bases in cool spring weather; maggots feed on roots 3-4 weeks; first flight roughly coincides with forsythia/lilac bloom.
biology.feeding: Maggots tunneling roots and germinating seeds

pests.damage: Wilting midday, stunted or collapsing seedlings, tunneled radishes and onion bulbs; seedcorn maggot kills germinating seeds in cold wet soil.
pests.favoring_conditions: Cool wet springs, fresh organic matter or manure worked in just before seeding.
management: Row cover from transplant/seeding in spring
Avoid incorporating fresh organic matter right before planting
pests.identification: Adults resemble small gray-brown houseflies about 5 mm; larvae are white legless tapered maggots in roots and stem bases. The three Delia species are near-identical as adults and are separated mainly by host and timing.
pests.scouting: Look for midday wilting, then pull plants and inspect roots and stem base for tunneling. Seedcorn maggot shows up as failed germination or hollowed seed in cold wet soil.
pests.phenology: Seedcorn maggot flight coincides with forsythia bloom; cabbage maggot follows roughly one to two weeks later at yellow rocket (Barbarea vulgaris) bloom. MSU Enviroweather uses about 300 DD base 43 F for spring emergence, completing near 564 DD; NEWA-style models place first cabbage maggot flight near 160 DD base 40 F with 50 percent spring flight near 250 DD, which is when covers need to be on.

biology.lifecycle: Low-flying fly lays eggs at the crown; larvae tunnel roots leaving rust-colored frass; two main flights (spring and late summer).
biology.feeding: Larval tunneling in the root surface

pests.damage: Rusty surface tunnels that ruin roots and invite rot in storage.
pests.favoring_conditions: Cool coastal climates, continuous carrot/parsnip/celery culture.
management: Row cover or insect netting for the entire crop
Rotate away from all umbelliferous crops
pests.identification: Adult is a shiny black fly 6 to 7 mm with an orange head and legs and clear wings; larvae are yellowish-white legless maggots tunneling just under the root surface, leaving rust-brown frass-filled scars.
pests.scouting: Yellow sticky traps placed low in the canopy near soil level, since adults fly low. Begin at the second true-leaf stage.
pests.phenology: Ontario muck-crop models use a 3 C soil base: first-generation emergence begins around 329 to 395 DD, second generation roughly 971 DD after the first. PNW guidance also uses the second-leaf carrot stage as the scouting benchmark.

biology.lifecycle: Striking red-and-black stink bug; adults overwinter in debris; keg-shaped black-and-white banded eggs in double rows.
biology.feeding: Piercing-sucking on leaves and stems

pests.damage: White blotches and wilting; can kill young brassicas outright in the South.
pests.favoring_conditions: Mild winters, weedy mustards as alternate hosts, overwintering debris.
management: Mustard trap crops destroyed with the bugs on them
pests.identification: Adults are shield-shaped, about 3/8 inch, black with vivid red, orange, and yellow markings. Eggs are pale barrels ringed with two black bands and a black crescent on top, laid in double rows of 10 to 13. Nymphs are rounded and black, gaining markings across five instars.
pests.scouting: Turn leaves to find the double-row egg clusters, and watch brassicas for white stippled blotches and wilting, especially near weedy overwintering mustards.
pests.phenology: Adults overwinter in debris and residue and emerge in spring to lay. Two to three generations across most of the range, more in the deep South. Confirmed host range extends beyond cole crops to bean, tomato, squash, potato, and okra, which is broader than the current hosts list.
pests.notes: Host range confirmed broader than cole crops: also bean, tomato, squash, potato, okra.
pests.us_regions: A southern pest historically, damaging in the Southeast, Gulf states, Texas, the Southwest and coastal California, where it can destroy fall brassicas outright. Its range has expanded steadily north and it is now a recurring problem in the mid-Atlantic and Pennsylvania. Rarely a factor in New England, the northern Midwest or the northern Plains, where winters kill the adults.

pests.scientific_name: Deroceras reticulatum, Arion spp., Cornu aspersum

biology.lifecycle: Night feeders sheltering by day under mulch, boards, and dense foliage; eggs in soil crevices; active whenever mild and moist.
biology.feeding: Rasping irregular holes, seedlings grazed flat

pests.damage: Ragged holes with slime trails, seedling loss, fruit pitting near the ground.
pests.favoring_conditions: Wet weather, heavy mulch, irrigated shade, mild winters.
management: Water in the morning so surfaces dry by night
pests.identification: Slugs are soft-bodied and shell-less, generally gray to brown; snails carry a visible coiled shell. Dried slime trails on foliage and soil are a reliable diagnostic even when no animals are found.
pests.scouting: Scout on cool damp mornings and evenings or by flashlight after dark. By day, check under boards, pots, mulch, and dense foliage. Board traps and beer traps are the standard extension monitoring tools.
pests.phenology: Not tightly seasonal. Cornu aspersum takes about 2 years to mature and lays up to 6 times a year, while Deroceras reticulatum matures in 3 to 6 months. Activity tracks moisture and mild temperature rather than discrete generations, which makes the row's '1-2 generations' figure loose but not wrong.

biology.lifecycle: Cannot survive northern winters. Adults overwinter along the Gulf Coast from Louisiana to Florida and ride southerly storm fronts north in May and June, arriving in the Midwest and Northeast in a single wave. Wedge-shaped bright yellow-green adults about 3 mm; pale wingless nymphs that run sideways when disturbed. Eggs are inserted into leaf veins and petioles.
biology.generations_per_year: 3-4 after arrival in the northern tier; continuous in the Gulf states
biology.feeding: Vascular feeding on leaf undersides; injects saliva that plugs phloem

pests.damage: Hopperburn: leaf tips and margins yellow then brown and go brittle, leaves cup downward and crinkle, plants dwarf. Beans bronze and stop setting pods; potatoes look drought-stressed and lose yield well before symptoms are obvious. Damage is from injected toxic saliva, not tissue removal, so a small population does real harm and the injury does not reverse.
pests.favoring_conditions: Hot dry weather after a June arrival flight; young succulent regrowth; adjacent alfalfa fields, which push a mass of leafhoppers into gardens the day they are cut.
management: Scout leaf undersides weekly from June; treat on nymph counts, not on visible hopperburn, which means the yield is already lost
Floating row cover on beans and young potatoes through the arrival flight
Do not plant beans or potatoes downwind of alfalfa, or expect a spike at each cutting
Insecticidal soap or pyrethrin on nymphs; conserve lacewings, lady beetles and spiders
Hairy-leaved or tolerant bean and potato varieties where available

biology.lifecycle: Small gray-green wedge-shaped adults 3-4 mm with six black spots on the head. Overwinters as eggs in small grains and perennial weeds in the north and as adults along the Gulf; most northern populations arrive as spring migrants carried up from the southern Great Plains. Nymphs pass through five instars in 3-4 weeks.
biology.generations_per_year: 2-5 depending on latitude and arrival date
biology.feeding: Phloem sap from leaves; over 300 recorded host plants

pests.damage: Direct feeding damage is minor and only matters at very high densities. The pest matters as the vector of aster yellows: a single infective leafhopper can condemn a carrot or lettuce plant, so scouting is aimed at the proportion of the population carrying the phytoplasma (the aster yellows infectivity index) rather than at raw numbers.
pests.favoring_conditions: Big spring migrations arriving on southerly winds; nearby small grains, alfalfa or weedy field margins, especially at cutting or drydown when leafhoppers move out; cooler summers, which favor phytoplasma transmission.
management: Row cover over carrots and lettuce through the spring migration
Control perennial broadleaf weeds that host both the leafhopper and the phytoplasma
Use the local aster yellows infectivity index, not leafhopper counts alone, to decide on sprays
Do not plant carrots or lettuce immediately downwind of small grains or alfalfa
Remove symptomatic plants so they do not become an in-garden source

biology.lifecycle: Invasive from East Asia, first found in Allentown, Pennsylvania in the late 1990s. Adults are 14-17 mm, mottled brown shields with white bands on the antennae and alternating light and dark bands on the abdominal edge. Overwinters as an adult in wall voids, attics and sheds, emerging in spring. Barrel-shaped pale green egg masses of about 28 on leaf undersides from June to August; five nymphal instars, the first ones black and red and clustered around the hatched eggs.
biology.generations_per_year: 1 in the northern range, 2 in the mid-Atlantic and south
biology.feeding: Piercing-sucking on fruit, pods, seeds and stems with a stylet that reaches deep into fruit tissue

pests.damage: Cloudy corky white or brown pithy spots under the skin of tomatoes and peppers, often invisible until the fruit is cut; distorted 'cat-faced' fruit; dimpled and aborted bean pods with shriveled seed; stunted kernels on sweet corn ears fed through the husk. Feeding wounds admit yeasts and rot organisms. Damage runs highest at field and garden edges next to woods or buildings.
pests.favoring_conditions: Gardens bordered by wooded edges, tree-of-heaven, or fruit trees; warm falls that build a large overwintering population; late-season plantings that stay green while surrounding crops dry down.
management: Scout fruit and pods at the garden perimeter starting mid-season, since infestation moves inward from the edge
Hand-pick adults and nymphs into soapy water in the morning while they are sluggish; crush egg masses on leaf undersides
Insect netting or row cover over pepper and tomato where fruit quality matters most
Conserve the samurai wasp Trissolcus japonicus and native egg parasitoids; avoid broad-spectrum sprays that wipe out the natural enemies holding aphids and mites down
Perimeter trap crops (sorghum, sunflower, okra) intercept adults before they reach fruit
Seal the house in fall; do not spray indoors for overwintering adults

biology.lifecycle: Overwinters only in Florida, south Texas, Arizona and similar frost-free areas, then moves north through the season and reaches much of the country by mid to late summer. Gray-brown moths lay fuzzy scale-covered egg masses of 50-150 on leaf undersides. Larvae are smooth pale to olive green with a wavy light stripe down each side and a distinct dark spot above the second true leg; five instars in as little as 24 days at warm temperatures.
biology.generations_per_year: up to 5-6 in the Deep South; 1-3 in the north as a late-season migrant
biology.feeding: Young larvae feed gregariously and skeletonize leaves in a web; older larvae disperse and chew large irregular holes, bore into lettuce heads, cole crop buds and growing points, and scar tomato and pepper fruit

pests.damage: Skeletonized patches with webbing early, then heavy defoliation and boring into hearts and buds. Damage concentrates at growing points, so a small number of larvae can destroy a lettuce head or a pepper terminal. On tomato as little as one caterpillar per 20 plants is enough to cause economic loss.
pests.favoring_conditions: Hot dry summers, weedy plantings with pigweed and purslane, and gardens that have been sprayed with broad-spectrum insecticides, which remove the parasitoids and the natural virus epizootic that normally crash populations.
management: Scout twice weekly for egg masses and small larvae; act at first or second instar, because large beet armyworms are notably hard to kill
Hand-remove egg masses and webbed skeletonized leaves
Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki) is only reliable on very small larvae; spinosad performs better on this species
Spray at dusk when larvae come out to feed
Control pigweed, purslane and lambsquarters in and around the garden
Conserve braconid and tachinid parasitoids, minute pirate bugs and damsel bugs; avoid broad-spectrum products
Row cover on young greens and cole crops during migration flights

biology.lifecycle: A 2-3.5 mm dark bronze to black snout beetle. Females chew a hole in a flower bud or small fruit, lay a single egg inside and seal it; the grub develops entirely within the bud or fruit, pupates there, and chews out as an adult. Egg to adult in about 2-3 weeks in warm weather. Adults live 2-3 months and continue feeding. Cannot survive freezing winters; persists year-round only in the southern tier and on solanaceous weeds such as nightshades.
biology.generations_per_year: 3-8 where it overwinters; continuous overlapping generations in season
biology.feeding: Adults puncture buds and fruit; larvae feed on the seed core and placenta inside the fruit

pests.damage: Bud and small-fruit drop is the first sign, and often the only one until harvest. Infested fruit shows a tiny dark puncture, turns prematurely yellow, orange or red, and drops; cutting one open reveals a frass-filled core and a grub or its exit hole. Because immatures are protected inside the fruit, sprays reach only adults, and once a planting is infested it is very hard to recover.
pests.favoring_conditions: Frost-free winters (Florida, south Texas, southern California, and the Gulf); nearby nightshade weeds; overlapping pepper plantings and volunteer peppers that bridge generations; long harvest windows.
management: Watch for unexplained bud and small-fruit drop and cut fallen fruit to confirm before assuming a nutritional cause
Pick up and destroy all dropped buds and fruit at least twice a week; this removes the next generation and is the single most effective home-garden tactic
Yellow sticky cards plus the aggregation pheromone lure to detect adults early
Destroy the planting promptly at the end of harvest; do not leave volunteer or ratoon peppers
Remove nightshade and other solanaceous weeds within and around the garden
The parasitoid Catolaccus hunteri gives some suppression; conserve it
In the north, this is a transplant-borne risk only: inspect southern-grown pepper transplants
pests.us_regions: Established and severe only where winters are frost-free: south and central Florida, the Lower Rio Grande Valley and south Texas, southern California and Arizona, plus Hawaii, with periodic outbreaks pushing into the Carolinas and Georgia during mild years. North of the freeze line it appears only as an ephemeral introduction on southern-grown transplants or shipped peppers and cannot overwinter, so northern gardeners should inspect transplants rather than plan for it.

biology.lifecycle: A wedge-shaped four-legged eriophyid mite about 0.15 mm long, invisible without a 14x hand lens or better, and usually diagnosed from damage alone. Egg to adult in about a week at 27 C, so populations explode. Overwinters on nightshade, bindweed, morning glory, petunia and volunteer tomatoes; carried into gardens on wind, tools, hands and clothing.
biology.generations_per_year: many, overlapping; a generation about every 7 days in warm weather
biology.feeding: Rasping epidermal cells of stems, petioles and leaf undersides, working from the base of the plant upward

pests.damage: Starts as a greasy bronze or russet cast on the lower stem and the undersides of bottom leaves, which then curl, dry and drop while the discoloration climbs the plant. Stems turn rusty brown and lose their hairs. Fruit exposed by defoliation sunscalds and may develop russeted skin. Heavy infestations kill plants outright. Damage usually shows once green fruit reaches about an inch and is easily mistaken for early blight, drought or fertilizer burn.
pests.favoring_conditions: Hot dry weather, low humidity, dusty conditions, and dense plantings; sheltered greenhouse and hoophouse tomatoes are particularly at risk.
management: Inspect the lower stem and the leaves just above obvious bronzing under magnification; recheck marked plants every 2-3 days, because the front moves upward fast
Sulfur dust or wettable sulfur is the standard control; apply at label rate, not above 32 C, not on heavy dew, and never within 2-3 weeks of an oil spray
Treat the whole plant including stems, and treat neighboring plants, since spread is by contact and wind
Pull and bag severely infested plants rather than trying to save them
Remove nightshade, bindweed and morning glory near beds, especially where the problem recurs annually
Wash hands and tools after handling infested plants; do not move from infested to clean plants
Predatory mites (Transeius montdorensis, Amblyseius species) give partial control in protected culture

diseases.name: Early blight
diseases.symptoms: Brown leaf spots with concentric target rings and yellow halos, starting on oldest leaves; stem collar rot on seedlings; leathery dark fruit-shoulder lesions.

favoring_conditions.moisture: Heavy dew, rain, overhead irrigation; alternating wet-dry
favoring_conditions.other: Nitrogen-stressed or heavily fruiting plants; inoculum survives on residue and volunteers

diseases.transmission: Splash-dispersed spores from infected residue and soil; seed-borne at low rates.
management: 2-3 year rotation away from solanaceous crops
Prune lower leaves, stake for airflow
Protectant fungicides (chlorothalonil, copper) at first sign
diseases.diagnostic_tell: Concentric dark-brown target rings inside the lesion with a yellow halo, always starting on the oldest lowest leaves
diseases.survival: Multiple years on infected debris and in soil; reports of over a decade under favorable conditions

diseases.name: Late blight
diseases.symptoms: Large greasy gray-green leaf blotches turning brown, white sporulation on undersides in humid mornings; firm brown fruit rot; entire plants collapse within days.

favoring_conditions.moisture: Extended leaf wetness, cool rainy spells, fog, humidity above ~90%
favoring_conditions.other: Living host tissue required; overwinters in potato tubers (cull piles, volunteers) in cold climates

diseases.transmission: Wind-blown sporangia travel kilometers; infected seed potatoes and tomato transplants start regional epidemics.
management: Destroy volunteer potatoes and cull piles
Immediate removal and bagging of infected plants
Preventive fungicides during cool wet weather
diseases.diagnostic_tell: White cottony sporulation on the leaf underside at the lesion margin in cool humid mornings; a damp-bag test brings the fuzz out within 24 hours
diseases.survival: No survival without living host tissue in most climates; overwinters only in infected tubers, cull piles, volunteers, or transplants
diseases.us_regions: Everywhere in the US in the right weather, but the epidemiology is regional. It overwinters only in living tissue: cull piles, volunteer potatoes, infected seed tubers, and frost-free southern areas including Florida and south Texas, plus overwintering greenhouse tomatoes. The Northeast, the northern Midwest and the maritime Pacific Northwest get it most seasons, arriving either on storm-borne sporangia from southern outbreaks, on infected southern-grown transplants, or from local cull piles, with cool wet summers driving the worst years such as the 2009 US-22 epidemic. The arid intermountain West and the Southwest see it rarely outside of irrigated potato ground.

diseases.name: Septoria leaf spot
diseases.symptoms: Many small circular spots with dark margins, tan centers, and tiny black pycnidia dots, starting on lower leaves after first fruit set; leaves yellow and drop upward through the canopy.

favoring_conditions.moisture: Prolonged wet foliage, rainy humid periods
favoring_conditions.other: Overwinters on residue and solanaceous weeds (nightshade, horsenettle)

diseases.transmission: Rain splash from residue; spread on hands and tools when foliage is wet.
diseases.diagnostic_tell: Tiny black pycnidia visible as dots in the tan lesion centers, and lesions stay small (pinhead to 1/8 in) rather than forming early blight's larger target rings
diseases.survival: Overwinters on crop residue and on solanaceous weeds (horsenettle, black nightshade); does not persist long in bare soil without residue

diseases.name: Fusarium wilt of tomato
diseases.symptoms: Yellowing and wilting of one side of the plant or one branch, brown vascular streaking inside the stem, wilt worst in afternoon heat.

favoring_conditions.moisture: Any; worse in sandy acidic soils
favoring_conditions.other: Soil-borne, persists many years as chlamydospores; ammonium nitrogen worsens it

diseases.transmission: Infested soil, transplants, tools, and moving soil; enters through roots.
management: Long rotation offers limited relief given persistence
diseases.diagnostic_tell: One-sided or single-branch yellowing with a sharply defined brown vascular ring in a cut stem cross-section, worst in afternoon heat
diseases.survival: Chlamydospores persist in soil 10+ years without a host

diseases.name: Verticillium wilt
diseases.symptoms: V-shaped yellow-then-brown lesions at leaf margins, midday wilt with partial recovery, tan vascular discoloration; slower and cooler-weather compared to fusarium.

favoring_conditions.moisture: Moist soils
favoring_conditions.other: Very wide host range (400+ species) and 10+ year survival as microsclerotia makes rotation weak

diseases.transmission: Soil-borne through roots; moved with soil and infected transplants.
management: Eggplant has no strong resistance: use grafted plants or clean beds
diseases.diagnostic_tell: V-shaped marginal leaf lesions with midday wilt that recovers overnight; not reliably separable from Fusarium without culturing, but runs cooler and slower
diseases.survival: Microsclerotia persist 10+ years, effectively permanently once established

diseases.name: Bacterial spot
diseases.pathogen: Xanthomonas spp. (X. perforans, X. euvesicatoria and others)
diseases.symptoms: Small water-soaked leaf spots turning dark and greasy, often with yellow halos, shot-holing in pepper; raised scabby spots on fruit.

favoring_conditions.moisture: Driving rain, overhead irrigation, high humidity
favoring_conditions.other: Seed-borne and transplant-borne; survives on residue

diseases.transmission: Contaminated seed and transplants, splash, tools and hands on wet foliage.
diseases.diagnostic_tell: Raised scabby (not sunken) fruit lesions; night temperatures at or below 16 C suppress it even when days are warm
diseases.survival: Persists on crop debris, volunteers, and weed hosts between seasons, and on or in untreated seed

diseases.name: Bacterial speck
diseases.symptoms: Tiny dark specks with yellow halos on leaves; pinpoint raised black specks on green fruit that do not penetrate deeply.

favoring_conditions.moisture: Cool wet spring weather, windblown rain
favoring_conditions.other: Seed-borne; declines in summer heat

diseases.transmission: Seed, transplants, splash.
diseases.diagnostic_tell: Pinpoint black fruit specks that stay superficial and never sink in, with faint yellow leaf halos; the halo separates it from bacterial spot and the shallow lesion from canker's bird's-eye
diseases.survival: Overwinters mainly in infested seed and tomato debris; only short-term free survival in soil

diseases.name: Bacterial canker
diseases.symptoms: Marginal leaf scorch (firing), wilting of leaflets on one side, stem cankers with yellow vascular tissue, and bird's-eye fruit spots (white halo, brown center).

favoring_conditions.moisture: Humidity, clipping and handling wounds
favoring_conditions.other: Systemic; a transplant-house disease at heart

diseases.transmission: Infected seed and transplants above all; spreads plant-to-plant on tools during pruning and tying.
diseases.diagnostic_tell: Bird's-eye fruit spot (brown center, white halo) together with wilting of leaflets on only one side of the leaf or stem
diseases.survival: Up to about 3 years in undecomposed tomato debris and months on stakes, cages, and tools; a poor free-living soil competitor

diseases.name: Tomato mosaic virus / tobacco mosaic virus
diseases.symptoms: Light-dark green leaf mottling, fern-leaf distortion, stunting, internal fruit browning; symptoms vary widely with strain and temperature.

favoring_conditions.moisture: n/a
favoring_conditions.other: Extremely stable virus persisting on tools, stakes, hands, and in debris for years; no insect vector

diseases.transmission: Mechanical: handling, pruning, contaminated tools and seed coats; tobacco products historically implicated.
management: Resistant cultivars (most modern hybrids carry Tm-2²)
Wash hands, sanitize tools (skim milk solution is a classic inactivator)
diseases.diagnostic_tell: Fern-leaf or shoestring distortion with light and dark green mottling, worse in cool weather, and no insect vector involved at all
diseases.survival: Infective in dried debris and on tools, stakes, and hands for a year or more, several years in some substrates

diseases.name: Tomato spotted wilt virus
diseases.symptoms: Bronzed curled young leaves, dark ringspots on leaves and stems, stunting, dramatic concentric ring patterns on ripening fruit.

favoring_conditions.temperature_c: warm seasons with heavy thrips flights
favoring_conditions.moisture: n/a
favoring_conditions.other: Reservoir in hundreds of weed and ornamental species; greenhouse bedding plants a common source

diseases.transmission: Only by thrips (acquired as larvae, transmitted by adults); not mechanical in practice, not seed-borne.
diseases.diagnostic_tell: Bronzing of the youngest upper leaves going to necrotic ringspots, plus concentric rings on ripening fruit; virus must be acquired by thrips as larvae and is then retained for adult life
diseases.survival: No meaningful survival in soil or on surfaces outside a living host or viruliferous thrips; carries over in weed and ornamental reservoirs
diseases.us_regions: Field-endemic in the Southeast, worst in south Georgia, north Florida, Alabama and the Carolinas where tobacco thrips and western flower thrips overwinter on weeds and the virus is a multimillion-dollar annual loss in tomato and pepper; also chronic in California and the Pacific Northwest. In the North and Midwest it arrives mainly on infected greenhouse-grown transplants and bedding plants rather than from field thrips, so buying clean transplants matters more than thrips sprays.

diseases.name: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus
diseases.symptoms: Strong upward leaf curling, small yellowed leaflets, severe stunting, flower drop; plants infected young set almost no fruit.

favoring_conditions.temperature_c: hot climates and seasons with whitefly pressure
favoring_conditions.moisture: n/a
favoring_conditions.other: Southern US, Mediterranean, tropics; moves north on infected transplants

diseases.transmission: Silverleaf whitefly (persistent); not seed-borne, not mechanical.
diseases.diagnostic_tell: Strong upward cupping of small yellowed leaflets with severe stunting and flower drop when infection happens young; whitefly-only spread, no mechanical or seed transmission
diseases.survival: Not soil-persistent; persists in the whitefly vector and in weed and solanaceous crop reservoirs
diseases.us_regions: Endemic where its whitefly vector overwinters: Florida, Georgia, the Carolinas, Alabama, Louisiana, Texas, and coastal southern California, with the worst pressure on fall tomato crops in Florida and south Georgia. It is a non-issue in the northern tier and the Midwest except as an occasional dead-end introduction on infected transplants shipped north, so TYLCV resistance is a must-buy trait for Gulf and Deep South gardeners and irrelevant for most gardeners above roughly the 37th parallel.

diseases.name: Cucumber mosaic virus
diseases.symptoms: Mosaic mottling, distorted shoestring leaves, stunting, warty mottled fruit; one of the widest host ranges of any plant virus (1,200+ species).

favoring_conditions.moisture: n/a
favoring_conditions.other: Perennial weed reservoirs (milkweed, pokeweed, ground cherry)

diseases.transmission: Many aphid species, non-persistently (acquired and transmitted in seconds, so insecticides fail to prevent it); some seed transmission in certain hosts.
management: Reflective mulch to deter aphid landing
diseases.diagnostic_tell: Shoestring, thread-like leaf distortion showing up simultaneously across unrelated crop families (cucurbits, solanaceous, legumes, greens)
diseases.survival: Not soil-persistent; carried over in perennial weed reservoirs and picked up fresh by aphids each season

diseases.name: Powdery mildew of cucurbits
diseases.symptoms: White powdery colonies on both leaf surfaces and stems from midsummer, leaves yellow then brown and crisp; fruit ripen poorly and sunscald.

favoring_conditions.moisture: High humidity but dry leaf surfaces; unlike most fungi it does not need leaf wetness, and rain actually inhibits it
favoring_conditions.other: Shade, dense canopies, late plantings

diseases.transmission: Long-distance windblown spores arriving annually in northern areas.
management: Potassium bicarbonate, oils, or sulfur at first colonies
Early planting to set fruit before pressure peaks
diseases.diagnostic_tell: White powdery colonies with yellow spotting on the opposite leaf face, and it infects without any free water on the leaf
diseases.survival: Conidia viable about 7-8 days; chasmothecia rarely reported in the US, so most seasonal inoculum blows in from southern source regions

diseases.name: Downy mildew of cucurbits
diseases.symptoms: Angular yellow leaf spots bounded by veins, turning brown; gray-purple downy sporulation on undersides in humid mornings; rapid canopy death, cucumbers hit hardest.

favoring_conditions.moisture: Leaf wetness as little as 45 min to 2 h at cool temperatures can initiate infection; humid nights and cool cloudy spells drive severity
favoring_conditions.other: Obligate parasite; overwinters only in frost-free areas and migrates north each summer (tracked by the Cucurbit Downy Mildew ipmPIPE forecast)

diseases.transmission: Long-distance airborne sporangia; splash locally.
management: Resistant cucumber cultivars (post-2004 resistance, e.g. DMR lines)
diseases.diagnostic_tell: Angular yellow lesions squared off by leaf veins with gray-purple fuzz on the underside in humid mornings, then rapid canopy collapse
diseases.survival: Obligate parasite with no soil survival in frost-prone regions; oversummers in frost-free areas and reinvades north each season

diseases.name: Angular leaf spot
diseases.symptoms: Angular vein-bounded water-soaked spots that dry, turn tan, and tear out leaving ragged holes; milky exudate droplets on undersides when humid.

favoring_conditions.moisture: Rain, overhead irrigation, heavy dews
favoring_conditions.other: Seed-borne; survives on residue

diseases.transmission: Seed, splash, workers and tools in wet foliage.
diseases.diagnostic_tell: Vein-delimited angular lesions that dry and tear out into ragged shot-holes, with sticky whitish bacterial ooze droplets on the underside when humid
diseases.survival: Over 2 years in plant debris, plus on and in seed

diseases.name: Bacterial wilt of cucurbits
diseases.symptoms: Individual runners wilt then the whole plant, without recovery overnight; cut stems may show sticky bacterial strands that string between the cut faces.

favoring_conditions.temperature_c: warm early season with beetle activity
favoring_conditions.moisture: n/a
favoring_conditions.other: Cucumber and muskmelon highly susceptible; watermelon essentially immune, squash intermediate

diseases.transmission: Only via cucumber beetles (feces into feeding wounds); overwinters in beetle guts, not soil.
management: Beetle exclusion with row cover until bloom is the control
diseases.diagnostic_tell: Cut a wilted stem near the base and slowly pull the faces apart: a thin string of milky ooze bridging the gap confirms it
diseases.survival: Overwinters only inside the gut of striped and spotted cucumber beetles; does not survive free in soil or residue

diseases.name: Anthracnose (cucurbits and beans)
diseases.symptoms: Sunken circular fruit lesions with salmon-pink spore masses in wet weather; angular brown leaf spots; dark sunken pod lesions on beans.

favoring_conditions.moisture: Warm rain and long leaf wetness
favoring_conditions.other: Seed-borne and residue-borne

diseases.transmission: Infected seed, splash from residue, workers in wet foliage.
diseases.diagnostic_tell: Circular sunken black fruit lesions oozing a gelatinous salmon-pink spore mass in humid weather
diseases.survival: Overwinters on the previous crop's residue and on or in seed

diseases.name: Black rot of brassicas
diseases.symptoms: Yellow V-shaped lesions from leaf margins with blackened veins, progressing to systemic vascular blackening and head rot.

favoring_conditions.moisture: Warm rain, overhead irrigation, humid weather
favoring_conditions.other: Seed-borne worldwide; survives 1-2 years in residue

diseases.transmission: Seed and transplants, splash through hydathodes and wounds, tools.
management: 3-year brassica rotation including brassica weed control
diseases.diagnostic_tell: Yellow V-shaped lesions starting at leaf margins and hydathodes with conspicuously blackened veins running through them into the vascular system
diseases.survival: Roughly 1-3 years in residue; UMN recommends a 3-year rotation as a buffer

diseases.name: Clubroot
diseases.symptoms: Wilting and stunting above ground; swollen distorted club-shaped roots that eventually rot.

favoring_conditions.moisture: Wet soils
favoring_conditions.other: Acid soils below pH 7; resting spores survive 15-20 years

diseases.transmission: Soil-borne resting spores moved on transplants, tools, boots, and drainage water.
management: Lime to pH 7.2+ before planting brassicas
diseases.diagnostic_tell: Swollen club-shaped root galls that are part of the root tissue itself, paired with above-ground wilting that does not match a vascular wilt
diseases.survival: 7-10+ years; recent work reports viability out to about 20 years with a roughly 4-year half-life

diseases.name: White mold (Sclerotinia)
diseases.symptoms: Water-soaked stem lesions with cottony white mycelium and hard black sclerotia inside stems; lettuce drop; bean stems bleach and shred.

favoring_conditions.moisture: Dense damp canopies, prolonged moisture at flowering
favoring_conditions.other: Sclerotia persist 5+ years; 400+ host species

diseases.transmission: Airborne ascospores from soil-borne sclerotia colonize senescing flowers first.
management: Remove infected plants before sclerotia return to soil
diseases.diagnostic_tell: Split a wilted stem open: hard black rat-dropping sclerotia embedded in cottony white mycelium inside the pith
diseases.survival: Sclerotia persist roughly 3-8 years in soil, some sources up to 10

diseases.name: Damping-off
diseases.pathogen: Pythium spp., Rhizoctonia solani, Fusarium spp.
diseases.symptoms: Seeds rot before emergence; seedlings topple with pinched water-soaked stems at the soil line.

favoring_conditions.temperature_c: cold soils for Pythium; warmer for Rhizoctonia
favoring_conditions.moisture: Overwatered, poorly drained media; low light and crowding
favoring_conditions.other: Reused unsanitized trays and garden soil in seed-starting mixes

diseases.transmission: Soil- and water-borne; contaminated containers, mix, and splashing irrigation.
management: Sterile seed-starting mix and clean trays
diseases.diagnostic_tell: A pinched, water-soaked, thread-thin constriction right at the soil line while the leaves above are still green
diseases.survival: Persists indefinitely in unsanitized soil, reused trays, and old potting mix until sanitized

diseases.name: Bean rust
diseases.symptoms: Small rust-red powdery pustules on leaf undersides, yellowing, defoliation before pod fill.

favoring_conditions.moisture: 10+ hours dew or leaf wetness
favoring_conditions.other: Late plantings and humid late summers

diseases.transmission: Windblown urediniospores; overwinters on bean residue.
management: Sulfur early if history of rust
diseases.diagnostic_tell: The rust-colored spore powder rubs off onto a finger or clothing, which no other bean leaf spot or blight does
diseases.survival: Teliospores overwinter in bean straw and residue, germinating the following spring

diseases.name: Common corn smut
diseases.symptoms: Silvery-white galls on ears, tassels, and stalks that mature into masses of black spores.

favoring_conditions.moisture: Drought or injury stress followed by rain
favoring_conditions.other: Mechanical injury (hail, cultivation), high nitrogen

diseases.transmission: Soil- and residue-borne spores infect through young tissue and wounds; spores survive years.
management: Galls are edible (huitlacoche), which is one way to feel better about it
diseases.diagnostic_tell: Silvery-white swollen galls on ears, tassels, or stalks that rupture into powdery black spores, unique among corn ear and stalk problems
diseases.survival: Teliospores viable in soil and debris for several years, commonly cited as 2-4+

diseases.name: Downy mildew of onion
diseases.symptoms: Pale elongated patches on leaves with gray-violet furry sporulation in humid mornings; leaf tips die back; bulbs undersized and store poorly.

favoring_conditions.moisture: Long dew, fog, cool humid spells
favoring_conditions.other: Overwinters in bulbs, sets, and volunteer onions

diseases.transmission: Airborne spores produced at night, released in morning; infected sets and volunteers carry it over.
diseases.diagnostic_tell: Pale elongated dull-green patches that grow a gray-violet felty spore layer specifically in the early morning after a humid night, unlike purple blotch or Botrytis leaf blight
diseases.survival: Oospores survive in soil and debris between seasons; also carries over systemically in infected bulbs, sets, and volunteers

diseases.name: Basil downy mildew
diseases.symptoms: Leaf yellowing bounded by veins that looks like nutrient deficiency, with dark gray spore fuzz on the underside; rapid total loss of sweet basil.

favoring_conditions.moisture: High humidity, leaf wetness, warm muggy nights
favoring_conditions.other: Arrived globally via seed around 2007; sweet Genovese types most susceptible

diseases.transmission: Seed-borne and long-distance airborne spores.
management: Wide spacing, morning water, maximum sun
diseases.diagnostic_tell: Interveinal yellowing on the upper surface with dense gray-purple spore fuzz forming directly opposite on the underside, visible with a hand lens or by backlighting the leaf
diseases.survival: Not known to survive without living basil tissue; airborne sporangia last only days, so carryover depends on contaminated seed or continuous production

diseases.name: Potato virus Y
diseases.symptoms: Leaf mosaic, crinkling, and vein necrosis; stunted potato plants with reduced yield; necrotic ringspots on tubers with NTN strains; mosaic and fruit distortion in pepper.

favoring_conditions.moisture: n/a
favoring_conditions.other: Carried between seasons in infected seed tubers; symptomless infections spread it silently

diseases.transmission: Many aphid species non-persistently (seconds to acquire, insecticides ineffective at prevention); infected seed potatoes are the main reservoir.
management: Mineral oil sprays reduce aphid transmission in seed potato production
diseases.diagnostic_tell: Mosaic and vein necrosis with stunting but no stem lesions, confirmed by necrotic ringspots inside cut tuber flesh with NTN strains
diseases.survival: Not soil-persistent; carries over in infected seed tubers and volunteers, which is why certified seed is the control point
diseases.vector_note: Green peach aphid is the most efficient vector; most current US field spread is by transient non-colonizing aphids (soybean aphid, corn leaf aphid, bird cherry-oat aphid, English grain aphid), which insecticides fail to stop

diseases.name: Root-knot nematodes
diseases.pathogen: Meloidogyne incognita, M. javanica, M. hapla and others
diseases.symptoms: Stunting, midday wilt, nutrient-deficiency look above ground; distinctive galls and swellings on roots; forked hairy carrots.

favoring_conditions.temperature_c: warm soils; southern species need 18+, M. hapla tolerates cool climates
favoring_conditions.moisture: Sandy soils worst
favoring_conditions.other: Wide host range; populations build under continuous susceptible crops

diseases.transmission: Soil-borne; moved with soil, transplants, tools, and water.
management: Mi-gene resistant tomato cultivars (note: Mi fails above ~28 C soil)
Rotation with grasses and marigold (Tagetes) cover crops
diseases.diagnostic_tell: Galls fused into the root tissue itself and cannot be rubbed off, unlike the loosely attached nitrogen-fixing nodules on legume roots; forked hairy carrots on root crops
diseases.survival: Eggs and juveniles persist in soil between susceptible crops, building under continuous host cropping, worst in sandy soils

diseases.name: Cucurbit yellow vine disease
diseases.symptoms: Foliage yellows and vines decline about two weeks before harvest; honey-brown phloem discoloration visible in a cut crown; plants wilt and collapse.

favoring_conditions.temperature_c: warm season with early squash bug activity
favoring_conditions.moisture: n/a
favoring_conditions.other: Sporadic; south-central US historically, spreading

diseases.transmission: Transmitted only by squash bugs carrying the bacterium; overwinters in squash bug adults.
management: Squash bug control from seedling stage
diseases.diagnostic_tell: Honey-brown phloem ring in a cut crown of a yellowing vine, without the milky ooze string of bacterial wilt
diseases.survival: In overwintering squash bug adults, not in soil

diseases.name: Iris yellow spot virus
diseases.resistance_code: none commercial; cultivars differ in tolerance
diseases.symptoms: Straw-colored diamond or spindle-shaped lesions on leaves and seed stalks, sometimes with green islands inside; lodging of seed stalks; reduced bulb size.

favoring_conditions.temperature_c: hot dry seasons with heavy thrips pressure
favoring_conditions.moisture: drought-stressed onions hit hardest
favoring_conditions.other: Volunteer onions and culls carry it between seasons

diseases.transmission: Only by onion thrips (Thrips tabaci); not seed-borne, not mechanical in practice.
management: Rotate away from overwintering onion fields
diseases.diagnostic_tell: Straw-colored diamond-shaped lesions on onion leaves and scapes, often with a green center
diseases.survival: In living hosts (volunteers, culls, overwintered onions) and viruliferous thrips; not soil-persistent

diseases.name: Spinach downy mildew (blue mold)
diseases.pathogen: Peronospora effusa (syn. P. farinosa f. sp. spinaciae)
diseases.symptoms: Dull to bright yellow irregular spots on cotyledons and leaves of any age; grayish-purple fuzzy sporulation on the leaf underside beneath each spot; spots enlarge, turn tan and dry, leaves curl and blight. Unmarketable at the first symptom on a salad leaf.

favoring_conditions.moisture: Extended leaf wetness, fog, drizzle, overhead irrigation; dense canopies that hold humidity
favoring_conditions.other: High-density baby-leaf plantings and continuous spinach cropping; new races appear steadily under the selection pressure of resistant cultivars

diseases.transmission: Airborne sporangia carried plant to plant and field to field by wind and splashing water; oospores survive in soil and residue; infested seed and infected transplants move it long distance.
management: Resistant cultivars, chosen by the specific race numbers they cover (resistance is race-specific and breaks down as new races appear)
Rotate resistance packages between plantings rather than growing one cultivar all season
Wide spacing and drip irrigation to break up canopy humidity
Disk under or remove crop residue promptly after harvest; control volunteer spinach
Preventive fungicides where allowed (mefenoxam, fosetyl-Al, copper) applied before infection
diseases.diagnostic_tell: Bright yellow blotches on the upper leaf surface with grayish-purple fuzz directly underneath the same spot; on spinach only, and cool wet weather.
diseases.survival: Oospores persist in soil and infested residue for up to three years; the pathogen also carries over on infested seed and on volunteer and overwintered spinach.

diseases.name: Fusarium yellows of cabbage
diseases.pathogen: Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. conglutinans (races 1 and 2)
diseases.symptoms: Lower leaves yellow, often on just one side of the plant, then brown and drop; leaves curl and twist toward the yellow side; brown streaking in the vascular ring of the stem and petioles; whole plant yellows, stunts and collapses. Seedlings can die outright.

favoring_conditions.moisture: Not moisture driven; warm soil is the trigger
favoring_conditions.other: Chlamydospores survive in soil indefinitely once introduced, so rotation alone does not clean a bed. Broccoli, cauliflower and Brussels sprouts are largely unaffected

diseases.transmission: Soil-borne; the fungus enters through roots and colonizes the vascular system. Moved on infested soil, tools, water, and contaminated transplants.
management: Type A resistant cabbage cultivars (durable single-gene resistance to race 1; race 2 can overcome it)
Keep the pathogen out: clean transplants, clean equipment, no soil moved from infested beds
Plant for cool-soil timing, spring or fall, in areas where the fungus is present
Fungicides do not control this disease
Grow broccoli, cauliflower or Brussels sprouts on infested ground instead of cabbage
diseases.diagnostic_tell: One-sided yellowing and curling of lower cabbage leaves with brown streaks in the stem vascular ring, appearing in warm soil with no wet-weather trigger.
diseases.survival: Chlamydospores survive indefinitely in soil once a field is infested; rotation does not eradicate it.

diseases.name: Phytophthora blight (crown and fruit rot)
diseases.symptoms: On pepper, a dark water-soaked lesion girdling the stem at the soil line followed by sudden permanent wilt with leaves still attached; root rot; dark leaf lesions and blighted shoots in humid weather. On cucurbits, fruit sitting on wet soil develops soft depressed spots covered in dense white yeast-like spore growth, then collapses ('melts'). Blackened crowns on all hosts.

favoring_conditions.moisture: Saturated soil, heavy rain, flooded low spots, furrow or overhead irrigation. Symptoms explode after a downpour
favoring_conditions.other: Poorly drained or compacted ground, flat beds, and fields with a history of cucurbits or peppers

diseases.transmission: Swimming zoospores move through soil water and splash onto crowns and fruit; long-lived oospores survive years in soil and cull piles; spread on equipment, boots, runoff, surface irrigation water, and infected fruit that looks sound at harvest.
management: Site selection and drainage first: never plant susceptible crops in low or flooded ground
Raised, domed beds with drip irrigation; never irrigate from a pond that drains an infested field
Rotate at least 3-4 years out of peppers, cucurbits, tomato, eggplant and snap bean
Tolerant pepper cultivars (Paladin, Aristotle, Archimedes types) hold against crown rot but not fruit rot
Rogue and remove infected plants and fruit off-site; do not dump culls near fields
Clean soil off tools and tires between beds
Labeled fungicides (mefenoxam where the population is still sensitive, plus alternated modes of action) as a supplement, never the plan
diseases.diagnostic_tell: A black girdling lesion right at the soil line with the plant wilted but leaves still green and attached, appearing within days of a heavy rain, plus cucurbit fruit covered in white yeast-like growth.
diseases.survival: Oospores survive several years in soil, cull piles and infested plant debris.

diseases.name: Aster yellows
diseases.symptoms: Carrot: yellow or reddish twisted new growth, a broom of hairy secondary shoots from the crown, masses of white hairy rootlets, bitter woody taproots that rot in storage. Lettuce: stunted heads, yellowed twisted inner leaves, pink to brown latex discoloration, failure to head. Generally, virescence and phyllody (flowers turning green and leafy) and stunting.

favoring_conditions.temperature_c: cool to moderate summers; transmission drops when days run above 32
favoring_conditions.moisture: n/a
favoring_conditions.other: Big spring leafhopper flights carrying a high aster yellows infectivity index; perennial weeds and biennial hosts hold the phytoplasma between seasons; over 300 plant species in 38 families are hosts

diseases.transmission: Only by leafhoppers, chiefly the aster leafhopper, in a persistent propagative way: the insect feeds on an infected plant, then needs roughly 2-3 weeks of latent period before it can infect, after which it stays infective for life. Not seed-borne, not mechanically transmitted, not spread by touch or tools.
management: Control perennial and biennial broadleaf weeds around plantings, which are the reservoir
Floating row cover over young carrots and lettuce during the spring leafhopper flight
Rogue symptomatic plants promptly, roots and all
Insecticides only when leafhopper counts and the local aster yellows infectivity index justify them; killing an already-infective leafhopper does not undo the infection
Do not site carrots or lettuce next to small grains or alfalfa that are about to be cut
diseases.diagnostic_tell: Witches' broom of hairy yellow shoots from a carrot crown with a mat of white hairy rootlets, or flowers turning green and leafy; scattered single plants, never a spreading patch.
diseases.survival: Persists in the crowns and roots of infected perennial and biennial weeds for years, and for life in infected leafhoppers; does not survive in soil or residue.

diseases.name: Potato common scab
diseases.pathogen: Streptomyces scabies, S. turgidiscabies, S. europaeiscabiei; S. acidiscabies causes acid scab
diseases.symptoms: Tan to dark brown corky lesions on the tuber skin, either superficial and russeted, raised and warty, or deep pitted. Cosmetic on the plate but disfiguring, and pitted scab cuts usable yield. Foliage looks normal. On beets and root crops, similar rough dark surface lesions.

favoring_conditions.moisture: Dry soil during the 4-6 weeks after tuber set; scab is suppressed by keeping soil near field capacity through that window
favoring_conditions.other: Soil pH above about 5.2 (common scab); light sandy or gravelly soils; fresh manure, lime, or wood ash raising pH. Acid scab breaks the pH rule and survives down to pH 4.0

diseases.transmission: Soil-borne and seed-borne; the bacteria persist for years in soil and on seed tubers, and pass through livestock manure. Thaxtomin toxin production drives lesion formation on young expanding tubers.
management: Keep soil evenly moist from tuber initiation until tubers reach about 1-1.5 inches
Hold soil pH at or below 5.2 in dedicated potato ground; do not lime, and skip wood ash
Tolerant cultivars (Russet Burbank, Superior and similar); none are immune
3-4 year rotation to non-host crops such as small grains, corn or alfalfa; avoid beets and other root crops in the rotation
Add organic matter to improve moisture holding; avoid fresh manure
diseases.diagnostic_tell: Corky russeted or pitted lesions on the tuber skin with completely healthy-looking foliage; worst in a dry year on limed or sandy ground.
diseases.survival: Survives for many years in soil, on seed tubers, and passes through livestock manure.

diseases.name: Gummy stem blight / black rot of cucurbits
diseases.pathogen: Stagonosporopsis cucurbitacearum, S. citrulli, S. caricae (formerly Didymella bryoniae)
diseases.symptoms: Wedge-shaped tan to brown blighting starting at leaf margins, often with a yellow halo and tiny black pycnidia in the dead tissue; water-soaked then tan cankers on the stem near the crown that crack open and ooze amber gum; on fruit, greasy water-soaked spots that turn black and sunken with pimple-like fruiting bodies (the black rot phase). Vines die back one at a time.

favoring_conditions.moisture: Long leaf wetness periods, high humidity, frequent rain or overhead irrigation
favoring_conditions.other: Wounds from cucumber beetles, aphids, powdery mildew and handling are entry points; dense unpruned vines; heavy fruit load and stress

diseases.transmission: Seed-borne, and survives one to two years in cucurbit residue and on volunteers. Splash and wind-blown spores in gummy exudate spread it short distances; the fungus also moves on workers and equipment through a wet canopy.
management: Buy seed produced in arid western regions or hot-water treat seed
Two- to three-year rotation away from all cucurbits, plus clean tillage of residue
Drip rather than overhead irrigation; do not work vines while wet
Manage cucumber beetles, aphids and powdery mildew to remove wound entry points
Remove infected fruit and vines; never leave culls in the field
Protectant plus systemic fungicides on a rotation of modes of action (this pathogen develops resistance to strobilurins and boscalid quickly)
diseases.diagnostic_tell: Amber gum oozing from a cracked tan canker on the crown or vine, with tiny black pycnidia peppering the dead tissue and wedge-shaped blight at leaf margins.
diseases.survival: One to two years in cucurbit residue and on volunteers, plus carryover on infested seed.

diseases.name: Cercospora leaf spot of beet and chard
diseases.symptoms: Small round spots 2-6 mm with a distinct reddish-purple to brown border and a tan center that turns ash gray as it sporulates; centers may drop out. Spots coalesce, older leaves blight and collapse, and the plant pushes new leaves from the crown at the cost of root size. Makes chard and beet greens unsellable fast.

favoring_conditions.moisture: Relative humidity above 90 percent, prolonged dew, overhead irrigation
favoring_conditions.other: Dense canopies after row closure; a full infection cycle takes 7-21 days, so it compounds quickly in a warm humid stretch

diseases.transmission: Overwinters as pseudostromata in infected crop residue and on beet-family weeds such as lambsquarters; conidia are splashed and wind-blown to new leaves. Low-level seed transmission.
management: Resistant or tolerant cultivars where the seed catalog lists a CLS rating
Two- to three-year rotation and fall tillage or removal of residue
Scout starting at canopy closure and pick outer infected leaves early
Wider spacing, morning drip irrigation, no overhead water late in the day
Control lambsquarters and other Chenopodiaceae weeds
Copper for organic plantings; chlorothalonil or a triazole on rotation where labeled, because C. beticola builds fungicide resistance readily
diseases.diagnostic_tell: Small round spots with a sharp reddish-purple border and an ash-gray center; the purple ring is the tell that separates it from bacterial and phoma leaf spots.
diseases.survival: Pseudostromata in infected leaf residue survive one to two years; also on Chenopodiaceae weeds such as lambsquarters.

diseases.name: Bean common mosaic virus
diseases.resistance_code: BCMV (dominant I gene; recessive bc-1, bc-2, bc-3)
diseases.symptoms: Light and dark green mosaic mottling with puckered, downward-cupped, narrowed leaves; stunted plants; few and misshapen pods; seed set cut sharply. BCMNV, or BCMV on a plant carrying the I gene under heat, causes systemic necrosis called black root: darkened veins, wilting, and rapid death of the whole plant.

favoring_conditions.temperature_c: 20-30 for mosaic; above 30 the I gene can flip to the lethal black root reaction
favoring_conditions.moisture: n/a
favoring_conditions.other: Saved or uncertified seed is the primary source; heavy spring aphid flights spread it from the first infected seedlings outward

diseases.transmission: Seed-borne at high rates (the main way it enters a garden) and pollen-transmitted; then spread plant to plant by many aphid species non-persistently, in seconds of probing, so insecticides do not prevent it.
management: Certified virus-free seed; do not save seed from a mosaic-affected planting
Resistant cultivars: pair the I gene with a recessive bc gene rather than relying on I alone, so heat and BCMNV do not trigger black root
Rogue mosaic seedlings as soon as they show, before aphids move through
Do not work through beans when foliage is wet or when aphids are flying
Reflective mulch and weed control reduce aphid landings; controlling aphids after the fact does not stop spread
diseases.diagnostic_tell: Puckered, downward-cupped, narrowed leaves with light and dark green mosaic on scattered plants from the first true leaves onward, tracing back to seed rather than spreading from a field edge.
diseases.survival: Survives in infected bean seed between seasons; no soil or residue survival, and no perennial host reservoir in most of the US.
